hints: Look at the top number in each symbol $^{40}_{18}\text{Ar}$, $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$ and $^{40}_{20}\text{Ca}$ and recall what that top number counts.
walkthrough:
Read the atomic symbols correctly**
Think of $^{40}_{18}\text{Ar}$ like a code. The bottom number is the proton number, the top number is the mass or nucleon number. Here all three show 40 on top, so start from that common value.

Link nucleon number to particles**
Nucleon means a particle in the nucleus, so protons plus neutrons. Saying they all have nucleon number 40 is the same as saying protons + neutrons = 40 in each case, even though the split between protons and neutrons is different.
Final answer: All three atoms have the same nucleon number of 40, that is the same total number of protons + neutrons.

hints: Compare the bottom numbers 18, 19 and 20 and work out what this means for protons, then for neutrons by 40 minus protons, and for electrons in neutral atoms.
walkthrough:
Work out each particle count**
In a neutral atom, electrons = protons = bottom number. Neutrons = top minus bottom. So $\text{Ar}$ has 18p, 22n, 18e, $\text{K}$ has 19p, 21n, 19e and $\text{Ca}$ has 20p, 20n, 20e.

State the full difference**
Because the proton numbers 18, 19, 20 are all different, every count is different. You must mention all three particles to get the mark, they differ in protons, neutrons and electrons.
Final answer: They have different numbers of protons, different numbers of neutrons and different numbers of electrons.

hints: Recall that $A_r$ is the weighted average of isotopic masses, so let % of $^{32}\text{S}$ be $x$ and % of $^{34}\text{S}$ be $100-x$.
Set up the average equation using the data: $(x/100 \times 32.0) + ((100-x)/100 \times 34.0) = 32.09$.
Solve for $x$ to find one abundance, then subtract from 100 to find the other and check which isotope must be dominant since 32.09 is very close to 32.0.
walkthrough:
Set up the weighted mean**
Picture $A_r$ as a balance point. If $x$ is the % of $^{32}\text{S}$, the rest must be $100-x$ for $^{34}\text{S}$. The average is: $$\frac{x}{100} \times 32.0 + \frac{100-x}{100} \times 34.0 = 32.09$$

Find the second abundance**
The two must add to 100%, so: $$\% \text{ }^{34}\text{S} = 100 - 95.5 = 4.5\%$$ This makes sense because 32.09 is only just above 32.0, so the light isotope dominates.
Final answer: % abundance $^{32}\text{S}$ = 95.5% and % abundance $^{34}\text{S}$ = 4.5%

hints: Recall that electrons fill the shell closest to the nucleus first, so think which $n$ value and which sub-shell is lowest.
walkthrough:
Follow filling from the nucleus outwards**
Lower $n$ means closer to the nucleus, lower energy and filled first. The very first orbital filled in any atom is $n=1$, s type, so the answer is simply $1\text{s}$.

hints: Picture the three directional orbitals $p_x$, $p_y$, $p_z$ and recall their characteristic two-lobed shape centred on the nucleus.
walkthrough:
Visualise a p orbital**
An s orbital is a sphere, but a p orbital has two lobes, like a dumbbell or figure of eight, with the nucleus at the pinch point in the middle. Sketch two symmetrical teardrop lobes touching at a point, with the axes through the centre.
Final answer: Dumbbell or figure of eight shape centred on the nucleus (two lobes on opposite sides).

hints: From $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^63\text{s}^23\text{p}^4$, identify which sub-shell was filled last and is therefore highest in energy.
Think why an electron furthest from the nucleus and most shielded needs the least energy to remove.
walkthrough:
Pick the outermost electron**
Ionisation always removes the easiest electron first, which is the one highest in energy and furthest from the pull of the nucleus. In $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^63\text{s}^23\text{p}^4$, the last part $3\text{p}^4$ is the highest $n$ and highest sub-shell occupied.

Explain in terms of attraction**
A $3\text{p}$ electron is in the third shell, well shielded by the inner shells and further from the protons than $1\text{s}$, $2\text{s}$, $2\text{p}$ or $3\text{s}$ electrons. Weaker attraction means less energy is needed to pull it away to form $\text{S}^+(\text{g}) + \text{e}^-$.

Final answer: orbital: $3\text{p}$
explanation: It is the highest energy occupied orbital / the electron is least strongly attracted to the nucleus so requires least energy to remove.

hints: Write the outer configuration of P (atomic number 15) as $3\text{s}^23\text{p}^3$ and recall that the three 3p orbitals are filled singly before any pairing.
walkthrough:
Count the third shell electrons in P**
Phosphorus is $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^63\text{s}^23\text{p}^3$, so the third shell has 5 electrons, 2 in 3s and 3 in 3p.

Apply pairing rules**
The 3s box holds a pair, draw $\uparrow\downarrow$ in the single 3s box. For 3p there are three equal energy orbitals, and Hund's rule keeps electrons unpaired if possible, so put one $\uparrow$ in each of the three 3p boxes, all spins parallel.
Final answer: 3s box: up-down paired arrows ($\uparrow\downarrow$). Each of the three 3p boxes: single up arrow ($\uparrow$ $\uparrow$ $\uparrow$).

hints: Compare the 3p boxes you just drew for P ($\uparrow$ $\uparrow$ $\uparrow$) with S which is $3\text{p}^4$ and must contain one paired box.
Think what happens when two negative electrons share the same small orbital and how that repulsion affects the energy needed to remove one.
walkthrough:
Spot the structural difference**
Phosphorus is $3\text{p}^3$ with three singly occupied orbitals. Sulfur is $3\text{p}^4$, so one of its 3p orbitals contains a pair: $\uparrow\downarrow$ $\uparrow$ $\uparrow$. Ionisation of S removes one electron from that pair.

Link pairing to lower ionisation energy**
Two electrons in the same orbital repel each other strongly because both are negative and confined together. That repulsion partly cancels the nuclear attraction, so the paired electron is held less tightly and comes off more easily. Hence first ionisation energy of S is lower than that of P despite the greater nuclear charge.

Final answer: In sulfur the electron removed comes from a doubly occupied / paired 3p orbital.
The paired electrons repel each other, making the electron easier to remove, so less energy is required.
